exercises.title: Say hello
exercises.prompt:
Write a function `greet(name)` that returns the string
`Hello, <name>!` - so `greet("Ada")` returns `Hello, Ada!`.

Return the string. Do not print it. Returning and printing are
different things, and almost everything you write from here on
returns.
hints: `return` hands a value back to the caller; `print` only writes to the screen.
An f-string puts a name's value inside text: f"Hello, {name}!"
exercises.solution:
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

exercises.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
exercises.prompt:
Write `to_fahrenheit(celsius)` returning the temperature in
Fahrenheit. The formula is `F = C x 9/5 + 32`.

Return a float. 100 degrees Celsius is 212.0 Fahrenheit.
hints: Translate the formula symbol by symbol: multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32.
Use `9 / 5`, not `9 // 5`. Integer division would throw away the fraction.
exercises.solution:
def to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

exercises.title: Split seconds into h:m:s
exercises.prompt:
Write `hms(total_seconds)` that turns a whole number of seconds into a
tuple `(hours, minutes, seconds)`.

`hms(3661)` is `(1, 1, 1)`. Every part must be a whole number.

tests.name: one hour one minute one second

hints: `//` divides and throws away the remainder; `%` keeps only the remainder.
divmod(a, b) gives you both at once.
exercises.solution:
def hms(total_seconds):
    minutes, seconds = divmod(total_seconds, 60)
    hours, minutes = divmod(minutes, 60)
    return hours, minutes, seconds

exercises.title: Initials
exercises.prompt:
Write `initials(full_name)` returning the uppercase initials of every
word, separated by dots and ending with one.

`initials("ada lovelace")` returns `"A.L."`.
Extra spaces between words must not produce empty initials.
hints: `text.split()` with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empties.
Build the pieces in a list, then `''.join(...)` them.
exercises.solution:
def initials(full_name):
    return "".join(word[0].upper() + "." for word in full_name.split())

exercises.title: Format a price
exercises.prompt:
Write `price(amount)` returning the amount as a string with a leading
dollar sign, a thousands separator and exactly two decimals.

`price(1234.5)` returns `"$1,234.50"`.
hints: An f-string can format a number as well as insert it - look up the format spec after the colon.
Format specs compose: f"{amount:,.2f}" adds separators and fixes the decimals.
exercises.solution:
def price(amount):
    return f"${amount:,.2f}"

exercises.title: Letter grade
exercises.prompt:
Write `grade(score)` mapping a 0-100 score to a letter:
90 and above `A`, 80-89 `B`, 70-79 `C`, 60-69 `D`, below 60 `F`.

A score outside 0-100 must raise `ValueError`.

tests.name: rejects over 100
rejects negative

hints: Check the invalid range first and raise, then the happy path reads top to bottom.
Order your comparisons from highest to lowest so each `elif` only needs one bound.

exercises.title: Leap years
exercises.prompt:
Write `is_leap(year)` returning True for leap years in the Gregorian
calendar.

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except centuries, which
must also be divisible by 400. 1900 was not a leap year. 2000 was.
hints: The whole rule fits in one boolean expression.
Write it as: divisible by 4 AND (not divisible by 100 OR divisible by 400).
exercises.solution:
def is_leap(year):
    return year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)

exercises.title: Sum up to n
exercises.prompt:
Write `sum_to(n)` returning the sum of every whole number from 1 to `n`
inclusive. `sum_to(5)` is 15. `sum_to(0)` is 0.

Write the loop yourself this time, even though a formula exists.
hints: `range(1, n + 1)` stops *before* the second argument, so add one.
Start an accumulator at 0 before the loop, not inside it.

exercises.title: FizzBuzz as a list
exercises.prompt:
Write `fizzbuzz(n)` returning a list of length `n`. For each position
from 1 to n: multiples of 15 become `"FizzBuzz"`, multiples of 3 become
`"Fizz"`, multiples of 5 become `"Buzz"`, everything else is the number
itself as an `int`.
hints: Loop from 1 to n inclusive and decide one position at a time with if / elif / else.
Test for 15 first. If you test 3 first, no number ever reaches the FizzBuzz branch.

exercises.title: Second largest
exercises.prompt:
Write `second_largest(numbers)` returning the second largest *distinct*
value in the list.

`[5, 1, 5, 3]` gives 3, because both fives are the same value.
If there is no second distinct value, return `None`.
hints: `set(numbers)` removes duplicates in one step.
Sort the distinct values, then index from the end - but check the length first.

exercises.title: Squares of the even numbers
exercises.prompt:
Write `even_squares(numbers)` returning a list containing the square of
every even number in the input, in the original order.

Use a single list comprehension.
hints: The shape is [expression for item in iterable if condition].
A number is even when n % 2 == 0; the square is n * n.
exercises.solution:
def even_squares(numbers):
    return [n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]

exercises.title: Middle three characters
exercises.prompt:
Write `middle_three(text)` returning the three characters in the middle
of an odd-length string of length 3 or more.

`middle_three("abcde")` returns `"bcd"`.
Anything shorter than 3, or of even length, returns `""`.
hints: The middle index is len(text) // 2.
Slice from middle - 1 up to middle + 2.

exercises.title: Tidy up a name
exercises.prompt:
Write `tidy(name)` that strips leading and trailing whitespace,
collapses any internal run of whitespace to one space, and
title-cases the result.

`tidy("  ada   LOVELACE ")` returns `"Ada Lovelace"`.
hints: split() then ' '.join() collapses whitespace in one move.
str.title() capitalises each word.
exercises.solution:
def tidy(name):
    return " ".join(name.split()).title()

exercises.title: Acronym
exercises.prompt:
Write `acronym(phrase)` returning the uppercase first letter of each
word joined together, with no separators.

`acronym("portable network graphics")` returns `"PNG"`.

tests.name: extra spaces
tests.code: assert acronym('  as   soon as possible ') == 'ASAP'

hints: phrase.split() gives you the words and drops the extra spaces.
Take word[0] from each word, upper-case it, and ''.join the letters.
exercises.solution:
def acronym(phrase):
    return "".join(word[0].upper() for word in phrase.split())

exercises.title: Top N by value
exercises.prompt:

highest first. Break ties alphabetically by name.

exercises.title: Positions of a value
exercises.prompt:
Write `positions(items, target)` returning a list of every index where
`target` appears. Use `enumerate` rather than counting by hand.
hints: enumerate(items) gives you (index, item) pairs as you loop.
Keep the index whenever item == target - a list comprehension with an if does it in one line.
exercises.solution:
def positions(items, target):
    return [i for i, item in enumerate(items) if item == target]

exercises.title: Pair two lists up
exercises.prompt:
Write `pair_up(names, scores)` returning a dict built from two parallel
lists. If one list is longer, ignore the extra entries.
hints: zip stops at the shorter of its inputs, which is exactly what you want here.

exercises.solution:
def pair_up(names, scores):
    return dict(zip(names, scores))

exercises.title: The mutable default trap
exercises.prompt:
This function is broken. Every call shares the same list, so results
leak between calls:

    def add_item(item, basket=[]):
        basket.append(item)
        return basket

Fix `add_item` so that calling it with no basket always starts a fresh
one, while still allowing a caller to pass their own list in.

tests.name: accepts a caller's list
tests.code:
mine = ['x']
assert add_item('y', mine) == ['x', 'y']
assert mine == ['x', 'y']

tests.name: no mutable default
tests.code:
import inspect
sig = inspect.signature(add_item)
assert sig.parameters['basket'].default is None

hints: Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined.
Use None as a sentinel and build the real default inside the body.

tests.code: assert describe(1, 2, 3, sep='-', upper=True) == '3 values | sep=- upper=True'

tests.name: rejects negatives

exercises.title: Divide without crashing
exercises.prompt:
Write `safe_div(a, b)` returning `a / b`, or `None` when `b` is zero.
Catch the exception rather than testing for zero first, so you see how
`try` reads.

tests.name: uses try
tests.code:
import ast, inspect, textwrap
tree = ast.parse(textwrap.dedent(inspect.getsource(safe_div)))
assert any(isinstance(node, (ast.Try,)) for node in ast.walk(tree)), 'safe_div should catch the error with try / except rather than test for zero first'

rejects out of range
rejects a negative age
rejects wrong type

exercises.title: Parse the numbers you can

Write `parse_ints(values)` returning a list of the entries that convert
cleanly to `int`, skipping the ones that do not.

hints: Put the try inside the loop, around only the one line that can fail.
None raises TypeError, not ValueError - catch both.

exercises.title: Count the non-empty lines
exercises.prompt:
A file named `notes.txt` already exists in the working directory.
Write `count_lines(path)` returning how many lines in the file at
`path` contain something other than whitespace.

Close the file when you are done - a `with` block does that for you,
even when something goes wrong while you read.

tests.name: reads the file it is given
closes the file
tests.code:
import builtins
real_open = builtins.open
opened = []
def tracking_open(*args, **kwargs):
    handle = real_open(*args, **kwargs)
    opened.append(handle)
    return handle
builtins.open = tracking_open
try:
    count_lines('notes.txt')
finally:
    builtins.open = real_open
still_open = [handle for handle in opened if not handle.closed]
assert not still_open, 'count_lines left the file open - a with block closes it for you'

hints: `with open(path) as fh:` closes the file even if something raises.
A line of only spaces is not empty until you strip it.
exercises.setup:
LINES = ["first", "", "  ", "second", "third"]
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write(chr(10).join(LINES) + chr(10))
with open("more.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write(chr(10).join(["one", chr(9), "two", "three", "four"]))
with open("empty.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    pass
with open("blank.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write(chr(10).join(["   ", chr(9), ""]) + chr(10))

exercises.title: Invert a mapping
exercises.prompt:
Write `invert(mapping)` returning a new dict with keys and values

exercises.title: Running totals
exercises.prompt:
Write `running_total(numbers)` returning a list where each position
holds the sum of everything up to and including it.

`[1, 2, 3]` becomes `[1, 3, 6]`.
hints: Keep one accumulator outside the loop and append after each update.
itertools.accumulate does this too - compare once yours works.
exercises.solution:
def running_total(numbers):
    out = []
    total = 0
    for number in numbers:
        total += number
        out.append(total)
    return out

exercises.title: Make it fast enough

from collections import Counter


def count_pairs(numbers, target):
    seen = Counter()
    total = 0
    for value in numbers:
        total += seen[target - value]
        seen[value] += 1
    return total

exercises.solution:
import logging


def make_logger(name, stream):
    logger = logging.getLogger(name)
    logger.handlers.clear()
    logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    logger.propagate = False
    handler = logging.StreamHandler(stream)
    handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s:%(message)s"))
    logger.addHandler(handler)
    return logger

def transfer_copies(conn, from_title, to_title, amount):
    try:
        row = conn.execute(
            "SELECT copies FROM books WHERE title = ?",
            (from_title,)).fetchone()
        if row is None or row[0] < amount:
            raise ValueError("not enough copies")

exercises.title: Spot a cache-busting Dockerfile
exercises.prompt:
Docker caches each layer until something it depends on changes. Copying
the whole project (`COPY . ...`) before `pip install` means every code
change reinstalls every dependency.

Write two functions.

`layers(text)` returns a list of `(INSTRUCTION, arguments)` tuples, one
per instruction, with the instruction uppercased (Docker accepts
`run` as well as `RUN`) and the arguments stripped. Skip blank lines
and comment lines (starting with `#`). A line ending in `\` continues
on the next line: drop the backslash and join the pieces with a single
space. Comments never appear inside a continued instruction.

`cache_busting_lines(text)` returns the 1-based line numbers where
each `RUN` containing `pip install` starts, when a `COPY` whose first
source is `.` came earlier in the same stage. Arguments starting with
`--` (like `--chown=app`) are options, not sources. A `FROM` starts a
new stage and forgets any earlier `COPY`.

tests.name: instructions in order
tests.code:
text = ('FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
'
        'RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
')
assert layers(text) == [('FROM', 'python:3.13-slim'), ('WORKDIR', '/app'),
                        ('COPY', 'requirements.txt .'),
                        ('RUN', 'pip install -r requirements.txt'),
                        ('COPY', '. .'), ('CMD', '["python", "app.py"]')]

tests.name: the good order is clean
tests.code:
text = ('FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
'
        'RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
')
assert cache_busting_lines(text) == []

tests.name: the bad order is flagged
tests.code:
text = ('FROM python:3.13-slim
# app code
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
'
        'RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
')
assert cache_busting_lines(text) == [5]

tests.name: continuations, options and lowercase
tests.code:
text = ('FROM python:3.13\ncopy --chown=app . /app\nrun apt-get update && \\\n'
        '    pip install -r /app/requirements.txt\n')
assert layers(text)[2] == ('RUN', 'apt-get update && pip install -r /app/requirements.txt')
assert cache_busting_lines(text) == [3]

tests.name: a new stage starts clean
tests.code:
text = ('FROM python:3.13 AS build
COPY . /src
RUN pip install build
'
        'FROM python:3.13-slim
RUN pip install /wheels/app.whl
')
assert cache_busting_lines(text) == [3]

hints: Write `layers` first, but have a helper also remember the line number each instruction started on; `cache_busting_lines` needs it.
Keep a flag, 'copied everything', set by a matching COPY and cleared by FROM. For COPY, the first argument that does not start with `--` is the first source.

exercises.title: Cache-aside with a time to live
exercises.prompt:
Write `TTLCache(loader, ttl, clock)` for the cache-aside pattern.
`loader(key)` fetches the real value (think: a database query).
`clock()` returns the current time in seconds; it is passed in so
tests can move time by hand.

- `get(key)` returns the cached value if it was loaded less than
  `ttl` seconds ago. Otherwise it calls `loader(key)`, stores the
  result with the current time, and returns it. An entry exactly
  `ttl` seconds old has expired.
- If `loader` raises, the exception passes through and nothing is
  cached.
- `invalidate(key)` forgets a key. Invalidating a key that is not
  cached does nothing.

tests.name: returns the loaded value
tests.code:
cache = TTLCache(lambda key: key.upper(), 10, lambda: 0.0)
assert cache.get('b') == 'B'

tests.name: loads once while fresh
tests.code:
now, calls = [0.0], []
def loader(key):
    calls.append(key)
    return key.upper()
cache = TTLCache(loader, 10, lambda: now[0])
cache.get('a')
now[0] = 9.5
cache.get('a')
assert calls == ['a']

tests.name: expires at exactly ttl
tests.code:
now, calls = [0.0], []
def loader(key):
    calls.append(key)
    return key.upper()
cache = TTLCache(loader, 10, lambda: now[0])
cache.get('a')
now[0] = 10.0
cache.get('a')
assert calls == ['a', 'a']

tests.name: invalidate forces a reload
tests.code:
calls = []
def loader(key):
    calls.append(key)
    return len(calls)
cache = TTLCache(loader, 60, lambda: 0.0)
cache.get('a')
cache.invalidate('a')
cache.invalidate('never-cached')
assert cache.get('a') == 2

tests.name: a failure is not cached

hints: Store the value together with the time it was loaded, so `get` can decide whether it is still fresh.
A dict of `key -> (value, loaded_at)`. Fresh means `clock() - loaded_at < ttl`; only write to the dict after `loader` has returned.

exercises.title: A token bucket
exercises.prompt:
Write `TokenBucket(rate, capacity, clock)`. The bucket starts full with
`capacity` tokens and gains `rate` tokens per second, never holding
more than `capacity`. `clock()` returns the current time in seconds.

`allow(cost=1)` first adds the tokens earned since the last call, then
returns True and spends `cost` tokens if there are at least that many.
Otherwise it returns False and spends nothing, so a request bigger
than the whole bucket is always refused but costs nothing.

tests.name: a burst up to capacity
tests.code:
bucket = TokenBucket(2, 4, lambda: 0.0)
assert [bucket.allow() for _ in range(5)] == [True, True, True, True, False]

tests.name: refills with time
tests.code:
now = [0.0]
bucket = TokenBucket(2, 4, lambda: now[0])
for _ in range(4):
    bucket.allow()
now[0] = 0.5
assert [bucket.allow(), bucket.allow()] == [True, False]

tests.name: never holds more than capacity
tests.code:
now = [0.0]
bucket = TokenBucket(2, 4, lambda: now[0])
for _ in range(4):
    bucket.allow()
now[0] = 100.0
assert [bucket.allow() for _ in range(5)] == [True, True, True, True, False]

tests.name: costs
tests.code:
bucket = TokenBucket(1, 4, lambda: 0.0)
assert [bucket.allow(3), bucket.allow(2), bucket.allow(1)] == [True, False, True]

tests.name: a refusal spends nothing
tests.code:
bucket = TokenBucket(1, 2, lambda: 0.0)
assert [bucket.allow(3), bucket.allow(2)] == [False, True]

tests.name: a slow bucket
tests.code:
now = [0.0]
bucket = TokenBucket(0.25, 1, lambda: now[0])
bucket.allow()
now[0] = 2.0
first = bucket.allow()
now[0] = 4.0
assert [first, bucket.allow()] == [False, True]

hints: You only need two pieces of state besides the settings: how many tokens there are, and when you last looked.
On each call: `tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) * rate)`, then `last = now`, then compare with `cost`.
exercises.solution:
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, capacity, clock):
        self.rate = rate
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.clock = clock
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.last = clock()

    def allow(self, cost=1):
        now = self.clock()
        earned = (now - self.last) * self.rate
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + earned)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False

exercises.title: A consistent hashing ring
exercises.prompt:
Write `HashRing(nodes=(), replicas=100)` that decides which node owns a
key, so that adding or removing a node moves as few keys as possible.

Use the `position(text)` helper in the starter: never `hash()`, which
changes between runs. Each node gets `replicas` virtual points on the
ring, at `position(f"{node}#{i}")` for `i` in `range(replicas)`. A key
sits at `position(key)`, and its owner is the node of the first
virtual point at or after it, wrapping round to the lowest point when
there is none.

Support `add(node)`, `remove(node)` and `node_for(key)`. `node_for` on
an empty ring raises `LookupError`. The order nodes were added in must
not change any answer.

tests.name: one node owns everything
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(['a'])
assert {ring.node_for('k%d' % i) for i in range(50)} == {'a'}

tests.name: an empty ring
order does not matter
tests.code:
keys = ['user:%d' % i for i in range(300)]
one, two = HashRing(['a', 'b', 'c']), HashRing(['c', 'a', 'b'])
assert [one.node_for(k) for k in keys] == [two.node_for(k) for k in keys]

tests.name: adding moves keys only to the new node
removing moves only that node's keys
virtual nodes spread the load
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(['a', 'b', 'c'])
counts = {}
for i in range(3000):
    owner = ring.node_for('user:%d' % i)
    counts[owner] = counts.get(owner, 0) + 1
assert sorted(counts) == ['a', 'b', 'c']
assert min(counts.values()) > 600

hints: Keep every virtual point in one sorted list of positions, with a dict from position to node.
`bisect.bisect_left(points, position(key))` finds the first point at or after the key; an index equal to `len(points)` wraps to 0.

exercises.prompt:
A file format starts with a 12-byte header, all numbers little-endian:

Write `read_header(data)` returning `{'version': ..., 'flags': ...,

tests.name: too short
wrong magic

hints: `struct` describes a layout with one format string: a byte order character, then one letter per field.
`'<4sHBxI'` is little-endian: 4 bytes, unsigned short, unsigned char, one pad byte, unsigned int. `struct.unpack_from` ignores anything after the header.

exercises.title: Slice records without copying
exercises.prompt:
Slicing `bytes` or a `bytearray` copies. Slicing a `memoryview` does

Write `split_records(buf, size)` returning a list of `memoryview`

tests.name: fixed-size records

parts = split_records(bytearray(b'aaaabbbbcc'), 4)
assert [bytes(p) for p in parts] == [b'aaaa', b'bbbb']

tests.name: an exact multiple
tests.code:
parts = split_records(bytearray(b'abcdef'), 3)
assert [bytes(p) for p in parts] == [b'abc', b'def']

tests.name: nothing was copied
tests.code:
buf = bytearray(b'aaaabbbb')
parts = split_records(buf, 4)
buf[4:8] = b'ZZZZ'
assert bytes(parts[1]) == b'ZZZZ', 'the slices must be views onto buf, not copies of it'

tests.name: rejects a zero size

exercises.title: A byte ring that pushes back
exercises.prompt:
Write `ByteRing(capacity)`, a fixed-size byte queue like a pipe's
kernel buffer. Allocate one `bytearray(capacity)` in `__init__`, keep
it in an attribute named `buffer`, and never replace it: the reads and
writes wrap round inside it. Raise `ValueError` if `capacity` is
below 1.

- `write(data)` stores as many bytes of `data` as there is free room
  for and returns how many it took. It never overwrites unread bytes -
  a full ring takes 0, so the writer has to wait.
- `read(n)` removes and returns up to `n` of the oldest bytes, as
  `bytes`. An empty ring returns `b''`.
- `len(ring)` is the number of unread bytes.

tests.name: oldest bytes first
tests.code:
ring = ByteRing(8)
ring.write(b'abc')
assert ring.read(2) == b'ab'

tests.name: wraps round
tests.code:
ring = ByteRing(4)
ring.write(b'abcd')
ring.read(3)
ring.write(b'xyz')
assert ring.read(10) == b'dxyz'

tests.name: counts unread bytes
tests.code:
ring = ByteRing(4)
ring.write(b'ab')
ring.read(1)
assert len(ring) == 1

tests.name: one buffer, reused
tests.code:
ring = ByteRing(4)
first = id(ring.buffer)
for _ in range(3):
    ring.write(b'abc')
    ring.read(3)
assert id(ring.buffer) == first, 'buffer must stay the one bytearray made in __init__'
assert len(ring.buffer) == 4, 'buffer must stay capacity bytes long'

hints: Track where the oldest unread byte is and how many unread bytes there are. Everything else follows from those two numbers.
The next write goes at `(start + size) % capacity`; a read moves `start` forward with `% capacity` too.

exercises.title: Typed rows with their errors
exercises.prompt:
Write `load_rows(lines)` for CSV text given as a list of lines. Line 1
is the header `id,name,amount`. Read it with the `csv` module, so a
quoted field may contain a comma.

Return `(rows, errors)`. Each good line becomes
`{'id': int, 'name': str, 'amount': float}`, with the name stripped.
A bad line is left out of `rows` and adds one `(line_number, field)`
tuple to `errors`, naming the first field that failed in the order
id, name, amount. A line with the wrong number of fields reports the

hints: `csv.reader(lines)` accepts a list of strings and gives you each line as a list of fields; a blank line comes back as `[]`.

exercises.title: An upsert you can run twice
exercises.prompt:
Write `upsert(table, incoming)`. Both are lists of dicts, and every
dict has an `'id'`.

Return a new list: for each incoming row, if a row with that id
exists, merge the incoming fields into it (incoming values win, other
fields are kept); otherwise append a copy. Existing rows keep their
order and new rows follow in the order they arrived. If `incoming`
repeats an id, the later row wins.

Do not change `table` or the dicts inside it. Running the same upsert
twice must give the same result as running it once. Raise
`ValueError` for an incoming row with no `'id'`.

tests.name: running it twice changes nothing
tests.code:
table = [{'id': 1, 'n': 1}]
batch = [{'id': 1, 'n': 2}, {'id': 9, 'n': 0}]
once = upsert(table, batch)
assert upsert(once, batch) == once

tests.name: the input is untouched
tests.code:
import copy
table = [{'id': 1, 'n': 1}]
before = copy.deepcopy(table)
upsert(table, [{'id': 1, 'n': 99}, {'id': 2, 'n': 2}])
assert table == before

tests.name: rejects a row with no id

`out = [dict(r) for r in table]` and `where = {r['id']: i for i, r in enumerate(out)}`; then `out[where[key]].update(row)` or append and record the new position.

exercises.title: Aggregate in chunks
exercises.prompt:
Data too big for memory is processed a chunk at a time. `rows` is any
iterable of `(key, amount)` pairs, possibly a generator that can only
be read once.

Write `chunk_totals(rows, size)`, a generator that reads `size` rows at
a time and yields one dict of `key -> sum of amounts` for each chunk.
It must be lazy: taking the first chunk must read only the first

rejects a zero size
